entries.title: Honey by Elizabeth Jenkins review – a rediscovered 60s classic of sex, money and power

entries.content:
‘A sweet white grape of a book” is how Virginia Woolf described Elizabeth Jenkins’s first novel, Virginia Water, published in 1929 when Jenkins was 24. Jenkins may have detected a condescending note. She was wary of Woolf, having been invited into the Bloomsbury inner circle and then (in her own view, at least) just as quickly dropped again. Jenkins soon regretted the novel’s publication, apparently afraid acquaintances might recognise themselves, and tried to get rid of as many copies as she could.

Fortunately she wasn’t long deterred, either by her uneasy dealings with Woolf or her anxiety about Virginia Water; her subsequent literary career spanned 70 years, though most of her books had fallen out of print by the time she died in 2010. Perhaps this reissue of her 1968 novel, Honey, will bring Jenkins back into fashion. It ought to.

No one could accuse this book of grape-like sweetness. It follows beautiful and mercenary Honey Harper who, at 30, after a divorce and a string of affairs with wealthy men, marries Roland Ismay. Professionally successful and morally vacuous, Roly seems a suitable choice, but Honey is restless, concerned that her power over young men is waning. So naturally, when Roly’s ex-wife dies and his 16-year-old son Brian comes to live with them, Honey decides to seduce the boy.

Honey is a monstrously compelling character, and the early sections of the novel have the ruthless bleakness of Richard Yates, though funnier. Jenkins is witty on the sexual politics of the era, from the male teacher whose distrust of female wiles is so intense as to be “akin to the ancient fear of witchcraft”, to the female characters – Honey’s rivals and friends – who are forced to reckon with the limits of their own sexual power when exposed to the nuclear-blast force of Honey’s. The ever complacent Honey, meanwhile, will be left staggering from the shock of Brian’s indifference, and it is her increasingly desperate attempts to get his attention that drive the plot.

But more than sex, this is a book about money. One of the first things we learn about Honey is that “from the time she was 15 it was clear that she had not only beauty, but the kind of beauty that makes men ready to put down hard cash”. Her avaricious mother looks forward to Honey making a marriage that will entail a life of “mink coats and diamond watches”, and the mink coat in particular is a well-deployed motif. One of Honey’s first acts when Roly is sent the money for Brian’s upkeep is to persuade him to spend the bulk of it on a new mink coat for her, a mistake that will prove costly in both senses of the word. Jenkins is good on the ways in which, for Honey, money functions both as an end in itself and also as tangible evidence of her sexual power through the gifts she receives from men.

Since Honey is the novel’s strongest draw, its impact is diluted when she recedes to make way for a focus on Brian. He is a compelling character too in his way, with his combination of vulnerability and self-possession, and does add an emotional heft to the novel that Honey herself can’t provide. Jenkins is brilliant at balancing savagery with poignancy, as seen in The Tortoise and the Hare, one of her only books to have remained in print. But in this novel the two halves don’t quite fit, and I would have sacrificed any amount of emotional heft for more of Honey’s unhinged self-interest. We feel her absence most keenly in the second half, by which time we’ve spent a bit longer than necessary with the Cresswells, the kind but regrettably well-adjusted family of Brian’s best friend. When Jenkins is so good at dysfunction, do we really want her frittering away so many pages on healthy relationships?

The novel comes so close to perfection, to the pitiless, glittering beauty of the antiheroine herself, that I wanted a little more from it. Still, what we do get is a delight, a whole bunch of deliciously sour grapes. We should all be thrilled to see it back in print.

Honey by Elizabeth Jenkins is published by Daunt (£11.99). To support the Guardian buy a copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Tonight the Music Seems So Loud by Sathnam Sanghera audiobook review – in praise of George Michael
entries.summary: The author blends teen memories and biographical details for a very personal tribute to the late singerWhen Sathnam Sanghera was a child, his older sisters fell under the spell of Wham!, the pop duo behind hits including Last Christmas and Young Guns (Go for It). Their brother soon caught the bug, becoming a diehard Wham! fan and following the career of singer George Michael into adulthood. In Ton
entries.content:
When Sathnam Sanghera was a child, his older sisters fell under the spell of Wham!, the pop duo behind hits including Last Christmas and Young Guns (Go for It). Their brother soon caught the bug, becoming a diehard Wham! fan and following the career of singer George Michael into adulthood. In Tonight the Music Seems So Loud, Sanghera blends memoir, biography and cultural criticism as he explores the life and work of Michael via themed chapters covering the singer’s sexuality, activism, addictions, his Greek Cypriot heritage and his songwriting prowess.

This is no objective trawl through the life of a distant pop star. Immersing himself in Michael’s world, Sanghera rides the same London bus route that he was on when he wrote Careless Whisper at 17 and visits the restaurant that once belonged to his father (Michael worked there briefly, until his dad fired him for mixing up the drinks orders).

Threaded through the narrative are vignettes from Sanghera’s life and his fandom, for which he was ridiculed frequently. When Michael was arrested for public lewdness in an LA public toilet in 1998, Sanghera was at university, where fellow students tacked the cover of a tabloid newspaper with the headline “Zip Me Up Before You Go-Go” on to his door.

The voice actor Homer Todiwala is the narrator who expertly navigates the book’s blend of the personal and biographical and captures the many contradictions of its subject. Michael was a private man who mocked his biggest tabloid scandals; a philanthropist who was quiet about his good works; and a teen pin-up who became one of the most celebrated artists of his generation.

Available via Picador, 10hr 24min

Further listening

A Court of Splintered Harmony

Sarah J Maas, Recorded Books, 12hr 1min

The sixth instalment of Maas’s all-conquering A Court of Thorns and Roses romantasy series finds an old enemy threatening the human lands. But will the Night Court be able to put aside its divisions and mount a defence? Narrated by Elizabeth Evans.

Firstborn Daughter

Katherine Ryan, Blink Publishing, 7hr 57min

The Canadian comedian examines “firstborn daughter syndrome”, or the quirks of eldest daughters that can lead them to organise and take charge, in this blend of memoir and social commentary. Ryan narrates alongside comics Joe Lycett, Aisling Bea and her eldest daughter, Violet.

entries.title: Patrick Radden Keefe’s London Falling named Waterstones book of the year
entries.summary: The word-of-mouth success of the journalist’s investigation into the death of a London teenager is ‘one of the defining features of the literary year’London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestselling investigation into the mysterious death of a London teenager, has been named Waterstones book of the year.The book follows the parents of Zac Brettler, a 19-year-old who fell from the balcony of a lu
entries.content:
London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestselling investigation into the mysterious death of a London teenager, has been named Waterstones book of the year.

The book follows the parents of Zac Brettler, a 19-year-old who fell from the balcony of a luxury London apartment after pretending to be the son of a wealthy Russian oligarch, as they discover the murky, dangerous underworld of the city that their son had been drawn into.

In a Guardian review, Ian Thomson called it “a scrupulously researched work of narrative nonfiction”. “Grimly absorbing from start to finish,” he wrote, the book “opens a window on to a world of financial dirty work and Walter Mitty-like fantasies of aspirational wealth.”

Waterstones’ head of books, Bea Carvalho, said its word-of-mouth success “has been one of the defining features of the literary year”. Reading nonfiction is “vital, enriching, gripping and the buzz surrounding London Falling has helped so many readers discover this,” she added.

Radden Keefe, a staff writer at the New Yorker whose previous book Empire of Pain won the Baillie Gifford prize, said that at heart London Falling “is a story about family – about parents and children, about the perils of contemporary adolescence, and about how little we sometimes know the very people we love most”. The book was shortlisted for this year’s Baillie Gifford prize.

Meanwhile, Taiwan Travelogue by Yáng Shuāng-zǐ, translated by Lin King, which won the International Booker prize earlier this year, was named fiction book of the year. Yáng said it was “especially precious to see this story about Taiwan embraced and adored by the booksellers at Waterstones”.

Is This a Plum? by Oscar-nominated director Dan Ojari and his eight-year-old son, Finn, was named children’s book of the year. The cut-out picture book began when the pair realised “a plum looks a lot like a hippo’s bum”, said Dan. “Me and my dad made this book together – it’s very easy to read and will probably make you laugh at least once,” added Finn.

The winners will receive the “full and committed backing of Waterstones shops and booksellers across the UK”, according to the company.

Also on the shortlist were Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke, Stations by Louise Kennedy, The Book of Birds by Robert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris, Redwood by Ben Macintyre, Land by Maggie O’Farrell, May We Feed the Kingby Rebecca Perry, Ottolenghi Simple Too by Yotam Ottolenghi and Verena Lochmuller, The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout and John of John by Douglas Stuart, among others.

Both the shortlisted titles and the book of the year are nominated and chosen by a panel of Waterstones booksellers.

Last year’s winner was The Artist by Lucy Steeds, while The Café at the Edge of the Woods by Mikey Please was named children’s book of the year.

  • London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe (Pan Macmillan, £22). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: The 4thWrite short story prize winner – a tale of teenage girlhood
entries.summary: Read Darkroom by Meher Iqbal – this year’s winner of the Guardian and publisher 4th Estate’s award for unpublished writers of colourMeher Iqbal wins 2026 4thWrite prize with ‘evocative’ coming-of-age story• Content warning: This story includes a description of a sexual assaultNadia and I lay on the asphalt road, playing our favourite game for the last time. My older brother Abdullah had taught it
entries.content:
Content warning: This story includes a description of a sexual assault

Nadia and I lay on the asphalt road, playing our favourite game for the last time. My older brother Abdullah had taught it to me when I was nine: lie down on a speed bump, legs long and both arms outstretched by your ears, making your body a long pencil. I was in the wrong position that day – it was so hot that the backs of my shins seared when they touched the road, so I had to bend my knees. Nadia wasn’t allowed to have her legs exposed anymore, so her linen trousers protected her. The game was intuitive – when you hear a car coming, roll down the slope and run away as fast you can. If you turned around only to find that the car was a decent way away, you were a baby. Abdullah never explained the underlying objective to me, but I think he enjoyed how much it agitated and scared adults at the same time. Simple and stupid, like most things he taught me at that age, but I liked that it gave me an opportunity to see just how fast I could run; the 100-metre track at school never drew out of me what running for my life did. Nadia didn’t care about any of that, but she humoured me anyway.

She and I locked our clammy hands together and raised opposite arms up. Sharp barbs of hair peeked out from the bottom of my T-shirt sleeve, and I wiggled my shoulder to coax the fabric down my arm. I had shaved for the first time a couple of weeks prior, just after my 13th birthday. Nadia told me to lather Radox shower gel on the hair first to prevent cuts, but I had still nicked my skin.

‘If someone tells on us for this again Zara, I swear –’ Nadia said without looking at me. She shaded her eyes from the sun with her arm, eyelashes crumpled against her skin.

‘They won’t. Plus my parents aren’t even home, I told you. There’s no one to tell on us to.’

She sighed and I sighed back mockingly. She reminded me of myself the previous week, when I’d agreed to sleep in my 8-year-old brother’s bed after we’d watched The Ring, but only after I’d doled out a few eyerolls.

We heard a low growl emerging from several feet away. Through the open windows of the car came the sound of LMFAO’s Party Rock Anthem. I wasn’t going to any parties at which I could enjoy that anthem, but nonetheless, it had been inescapable all summer.

‘Ready?’ I asked.

‘It sounds close – on the count of three this time,’ Nadia said, instead of our usual five.

I counted down, scrunching my eyes shut so I could focus on the rumbles of the car. On one, I heard it come to a halt, expelling a gravely noise. I trundled down the speed bump, dragging Nadia with me at first and then letting go of her hand because she was running slower than me, like always. I heard her footsteps behind me as I bounded down the road. It was a few seconds before I noticed I couldn’t hear Nadia anymore and spun around on my heels, gasping for air.

She was going in the wrong direction, walking back to the speed bump. Looking at her from behind, I could still tell she was smiling. Her waist-length hair swished in the air as she bobbed her head, but I noticed her shoulders had wilted inwards like they always did when she was shy. And she was shy because the person who had been driving the car, the person I’d expected to be mid-tirade because of our silliness, was Sami.

Sami was a 17-year-old boy we had always known. Our mothers were friends in the way that justified mutual invites to big daawats but little contact outside of them. Nadia and I had been at the same girls’ school since we were 4, so Sami was one of the only boys we knew that wasn’t a relative. He got his driving licence that summer and drove a cobalt blue Ford Fiesta that made the sky look pale. No car had ever been cooler. Neither Nadia nor I knew him very well, seeing progressively less of him as we got older. But he saved me once when I was 7 years old.

A group of us had been playing darkroom at his house – hide and seek in the dark – and I was doing my best to hide my panic. I was still used to my mother leaving my bedroom door wide open when I went to sleep. When the lights went off in Sami’s parents’ room, I waited for my sight to adjust to the darkness and hoped the slit of light under the door would draw someone’s outline. At the very least, I prayed to see the blobs of blurry colour that comforted me when I closed my eyes. When neither happened, tears dribbled down my face and I sniffled quietly, but Sami heard me. ‘Let’s hide together,’ he whispered. Even in the dark, it felt like he was looking right at me, every corner of my fear exposed. He guided me by the arm to the nook between his parents’ bedroom and their ensuite. I wasn’t scared anymore – just mortified – and I didn’t know which was worse, so tears continued to soak my cheeks. We were the last to be found, and when the lights went on, he jumped up so no one could see me and shouted, ‘We won!’ I had brothers, I knew there’d be a catch – so I waited for him to recant his kindness. But he never did.

I walked back to join them now, bruised that Nadia hadn’t called me when she’d noticed Sami. He towered over her, about a foot taller than I remembered him. He stood with his legs wide to prove that he knew what to do with this new body of his. But his posture betrayed him, his back crooked and unsure of how to hold him up. His forehead was dotted with tiny bumps punctuated by angrier, redder ones that he’d tried to cover with his hair; they peeked out stubbornly anyway. But his jaw was sharper now, and he still had the longest, thickest eyelashes of anyone I’d ever seen. I became aware he’d just seen me sprinting like the 7-year-old he remembered me as, limbs flailing through the air. The thought was embarrassing enough that it sparked a counter-productive urge to turn and run away from him again. I searched for something to do with myself, settling on peeling sticky baby hairs from the nape of my neck and twisting them around my finger.

‘What are you two playing at?’ he laughed.

‘It was Zara’s idea,’ Nadia said, smiling with an ease that I wished I could snatch from her.

‘It was Abdullah’s actually,’ I said quickly.

‘Your brother told you and Nadia to go out and lie on the road?’

‘No,’ I said. My underarms moistened and I yanked my sleeves down. I wasn’t far off Sami’s height, and I felt shy having to look him in the eye as I explained myself. ‘Sorry, I meant my brother taught me the game.’

‘How d’you win?’ Sami asked.

‘Just like, don’t die,’ Nadia said.

‘You’re welcome then for not killing you.’

They both laughed and Nadia’s gaze was direct, her eyes sparkly. When Sami said bye before he got back into his car, he addressed us both but only looked at her.

As he drove off, I squealed at Nadia, ‘Why did you tell him it was my idea?’

‘Because it was! And who cares, anyway?’ Nadia said.

‘Obviously you care, that’s why you put it on me.’

And I cared too – I cared that Sami had caught us in the middle of a game that now not only felt silly, but uninspired. I cared that I had appeared juvenile in front of him, a charming older boy who I wanted to see me as an equal – who clearly saw Nadia as an equal. It was fine for her – at least she didn’t look like a child, even when she acted like one.

It was about five months prior that I’d wiped blood from between my legs for the first time and wondered if it meant I would turn pretty. Nothing else had happened yet to indicate the transformation. But when Nadia got her period, I looked at her doll-like face and her doe eyes, framed by angular eyebrows and eyelashes that looked curled – and realised that for her, there was nothing else left to happen. The excruciating anticipation I felt was a feeling she’d blissfully avoided; she had always looked exactly as she should. Nadia wasn’t just lovely in the way that every child is – she was pretty.

I had only cared about turning pretty at all as a last resort, when there appeared to be no other choice. I had grown up a worthy match for my older brother, whether we were racing, play-fighting or actually fighting. But as his voice dropped and his limbs grew spindly, I found myself falling short. I panted to keep up with him when he ran and struggled to shove past him when he blocked the passenger door of our mother’s Toyota. I tried so desperately to ignore it, until we were swimming one day and he playfully dunked my head in the pool. I wriggled for a few seconds like usual but realised I wasn’t moving up this time; Abdullah’s hands felt clamped on my head, and my body was locked underwater. My eyes burned from the chlorine and my fists were tight as I tried to thrust my head up. When he unstuck his palms from my crown and my body bounced back into the air, I smacked his chest and shouted, ‘That’s not fair!’ Then I hit him again to produce a sound from the impact that satisfied me more, but it was no use.

I realised then that whatever was waiting for me when I got to Abdullah’s age excluded strength and brawn. I would never again match my brother, or any boys, so it followed that one day I would match girls like Nadia. I had to fit somewhere.

But my body hadn’t cooperated with that task. It grew in all the directions and ways I didn’t want it to. I got taller, taller than all the girls and some of the boys my age. My stomach puffed out, preparing flesh to spread to hips that didn’t widen. Dark whiskers started sprouting on my upper lip and I immediately resented the chin-length hair I’d always had; I wanted long, cascading hair where it was actually meant to be, to detract attention from where it shouldn’t.

And my period went missing. I hadn’t had another one since my first, so Mama told me I didn’t have to throw out my shorts for the summer. My soft thighs, my knees that were so knobbly their contours and dips resembled a face – they weren’t worth shielding yet. It was probably a false start, Mama said. She always had a habit of sprinkling salt in wounds she couldn’t even see.

‘I don’t know why you were trying so hard to impress him,’ I said to Nadia after Sami drove away. ‘Mama said she saw him with a girl in his car a few weeks ago. A girl his age.’ This was a lie. Nadia might have been successful in impressing him, but I didn’t want her to think so.

‘Was she white?’

‘Yes,’ I said. I wanted to give the most off-putting answer, but I wasn’t sure if that was it.

‘Doesn’t matter then,’ Nadia said confidently. I didn’t ask what she meant by it, because I didn’t want to admit she understood something I didn’t.

Instead I said clumsily, ‘Yes it does.’

‘Whatever. What star sign do you think he is?’ Nadia asked. She’d started fixating on what she could learn about herself from her horoscope over the past few months.

‘That’s haram,’ I said.

‘Zara,’ Nadia said, elongating the vowels of my name and reaching up to wrap her arm around my shoulder. ‘Stop being such a bitch,’ she teased. We’d recently started trialling cursing, and it still sounded unnatural coming out of our mouths.

I rolled my eyes and let her drag us back to my house. I thought about asking her to play our game again, but the moment had passed.

A week later, there was a fundraiser in our local community hall for the victims of the Sindh floods in Pakistan. I usually liked going to events like that, as long as Nadia was there, but this time I hoped she wouldn’t be. We’d spent most days of the summer together so far, but that week, I made excuses when she’d texted to hang out.

‘We’re leaving, Zara!’ Mama yelled from downstairs. I took a kajal crayon from her dressing table and dragged it along my waterline like I’d watched her do for years. My eyes watered instantly. Fat droplets of water, tinged grey from the kajal, spilled out of my eyes and left tracks in the Collection 2000 concealer I’d smeared over my face.

Abdullah crashed into the room. ‘Zara, Mama’s going mad. Hurry up.’ Then, ‘Your face looks like a football pitch mate,’ he added. ‘What is that?’

‘Piss off!’ I slammed the door, seething at the accuracy of his comparison.

I frantically dabbed the damp lines on my face with a cotton pad and focused the kajal on my lids instead. I couldn’t manoeuvre the thick tip of the crayon close enough to my eyelashes, so a ribbon of skin remained naked beneath my liner. I hurried into the car with my family and stared out of the window for the whole journey, hoping none of them would comment on my darkly rimmed eyes. I felt like crying, and I didn’t know why. Perhaps it felt embarrassing to try so hard and suspect I was going to fail anyway.

Nadia was standing outside, waiting dutifully for her mother to finish greeting people before they went inside the hall. Her lips were stained rose, and that was the only bit of makeup she had on. She ran her fingers through her hair, and it poured down her back. I had originally straightened my own hair flat against my head, but it accentuated the moon shape of my face, so I weaved it into two plaits to create loose waves instead. It was too short for that to work properly though, and I ended up with sad crimps running down the bottom three inches. I had almost tugged clumps out of my scalp in frustration.

When Nadia saw me, she yelled, ‘Hey!’ and shuffled over, and I didn’t meet her halfway. ‘Where have you been this week? I’ve been bored out of my mind.’

‘Just, busy,’ I hummed.

‘Doing what?’

Before I could invent activities, she said, ‘You know, Sami’s here as well today.’

‘Is he?’ I looked around immediately, but Nadia grabbed my arm to reclaim my attention.

‘I’m going to try and talk to him again,’ she said in a low voice. The way she grinned, I could tell she expected me to return the gesture.

I stamped my lips together and said, ‘I saw him again you know, with that white girl.’ She was even real to me now – petite, with a helix piercing and light brown hair she insisted was blonde. She and Sami met in the park after school, and she smoked cigarettes without coughing.

‘I thought you said your mum saw him, not you.’ Nadia’s face scrunched and the image of the white girl in my head suddenly had a thick line scrawled over it.

‘That’s what I meant, my mum saw him again.’

Nadia raised her eyebrows and looked away. Her silent knowing made my skin itch.

‘Well anyway. I’ll see you inside then,’ Nadia said, rejoining her mother. The brightness of her face had dimmed slightly, and in that moment, I wished I didn’t care about any of it – what Sami thought of me, what he thought of Nadia, how I might magically swap those opinions – because it was making me mean. But I did care, and I couldn’t stop caring, so I couldn’t stop being mean. I didn’t know how to do one without the other.

When my family and I entered the hall, I scanned the room and found Sami instantly. His hair looked longer and flopped on either side of his face. He was greeting aunties with ease. He was speaking in Urdu; I could tell by the way they beamed at him. When he’d finished, he walked down the hall and towards the doors.

He brushed his hand against Nadia’s back as he went, without even looking at her. It looked like an accident to me then, but that was before I knew it’s never an accident.

Nadia’s cheeks bloomed pink, matching her lipstick. Her gaze followed him, fixed on the back of his head. Then, Sami turned for a split second to give her a perfect crescent-moon smile, his mouth closed, before leaving the room. I looked around to see if anyone else had seen what I had. Someone might have seen the brush of Sami’s hand, or his smile, but no one else was studying them for long enough to notice the quietly bold combination of both. Nadia played with her napkin for a moment before focusing on the glass of Sprite in front of her, staring so intently I thought she might be counting the bubbles, another one of our games. But then she got up, whispered something to her mother and walked out of the hall.

Before I knew what I was doing, I was following her. My pace stuttered into a sort of walk-run as I tried to strike a balance between keeping up with Nadia and ensuring she didn’t realise I was behind her.

I stopped when I got just outside the hall and pressed my phone to my ear like I had a crucial call to take, when the only people who ever called me were either inside the hall or currently strolling through the car park with the boy who’d saved me playing darkroom. For the first and last time, I longed for a cold call – anything to make my performance feel less humiliating.

Nadia and Sami walked into the stripes of pink and purple that flooded the sky. He said something and she threw her head back and laughed. It can’t have been that funny, I thought, knowing that I would’ve laughed the same if I’d been the one walking off into the sunset with him.

I saw his cobalt blue Ford Fiesta in the distance, and there were a couple of parking spots between my family’s car and his. Nadia slowed down her stride for a moment and looked back at the hall. She looked nervous – that she’d be caught alone with a boy, I assumed at the time. Now I wonder if perhaps, by then, she already knew. Like she seemed to know everything before I did.

I’d been jealous of Nadia before of course – like when her parents bought her a new phone, when I’d only ever had Abdullah’s scratched hand-me-downs. But this jealousy was thornier. It came from something she was, not something she had. She was a girl fit to go into boys’ cars with them and do whatever it was that they were about to do. I wasn’t, and I probably never would be. I’d always be messing around on the speed bumps, on my own now.

I slotted my phone inside my pocket and skulked after them. I didn’t know what I was looking for, but my legs carried me, and I let them. As I got closer, I crouched behind Mama’s Toyota – that way, if anyone saw me, I could say I was retrieving something from the car. A pad, that’d be a good way to shut anyone up. I poked my head out to watch Sami and Nadia, who by that point were sat inside his car.

I could only see the back of Sami’s head as he faced Nadia in his passenger seat. She glanced beyond him for a moment, out of the window, and again, I assumed she was keeping lookout, making sure they didn’t get caught.

And then, it happened quickly.

Sami lurched forwards, and it didn’t look like it did in films and TV shows. His face hit hers, and I thought their noses must’ve collided before their lips did. As Sami’s torso jammed into Nadia’s, she clutched his shoulders tightly – did that mean she was enjoying it? He clasped her cheeks, and I thought it looked like he’d wanted to kiss her for a while.

Then Nadia uncurled her fingers from his shoulders, and I waited for them to find Sami’s face, to cup his cheeks in turn – she’d probably wanted to kiss him for a while too. But they didn’t find his face. Instead, Nadia shoved her palms against Sami’s shoulders. And that didn’t look familiar either.

I waited a few seconds without knowing what I was waiting for – anything that would indicate I’d misunderstood.

Nadia rammed her open hands into Sami’s shoulders again. It must’ve been harder that time because he rebounded an inch. But then he pushed back into her face, and there was no doubting it anymore.

The legs that had carried me all the way outside turned to noodles. All the fantasies I’d had about how slick I’d be in crisis, how fast and agile, were worthless. All that time I’d spent running, running from cars, running to beat my brother, and now I couldn’t even walk. I wished I’d never let go of Nadia’s hand that day we’d bumped into Sami, and that we’d run so far away from that tacky blue car that we couldn’t see it anymore.

I swallowed the beginnings of a call for help, realising that Nadia would get told off for being in the car with him in the first place. I imagined wrenching the door open and hitting him all over, but I remembered how little that meant coming from my body now. I felt my stomach plunge so low in my gut, it pulled me closer to the ground.

And on the ground, I found my answer. A sharp, angular rock the size of a golf ball. It’d jolt him enough to get him off her, and she could get out and run away. I picked it up and slithered around Mama’s car, so I was on the other side now. I threw the rock overarm like a cricket ball, praying it’d fly far enough to hit Sami’s car.

It did. It hit the window squarely in the centre. And it did jolt Sami – he tore himself from Nadia’s face and turned at the exact same moment that the glass broke, leaving a jagged hole encircled by a spider web of cracks. He screamed a croaky scream that would’ve made me laugh had I been able to expel any sound at all. And then he saw me, and his scream wasn’t funny anymore.

‘What the fuck,’ he shouted. He flailed his arms in anger, and I saw cherry red blood streaming from a cut in his arm.

Bile soured my throat and burned as I gulped it down. I didn’t know what I’d expected to happen, but it wasn’t this.

‘Zara! Was that you?’

Nadia came running towards me. Her lipstick had smudged around the corners of her mouth, and her skin had the sheen of sweat or tears – it could have been either. I wished I’d hurt Sami worse.

The fear on her face was unlike the kind I’d seen before, the kind prompted by funfair rides and snarling big dogs. No, this was a fear that couldn’t belong to a child. It was entirely grown, fully realised.

She grabbed my hand and dragged me with her. We went for the outside gate of the community hall, as though we could’ve run from what was coming.

I heard Sami shouting behind us, a clamour of curse words. And then I heard the voice of an adult.

‘What on earth is going on out here?’

It was Nadia that let go of my hand and turned around first.

Sami’s mother stood before us, demanding an answer. Nadia’s mum, Mina Aunty, trailed several steps behind.

‘It was the other one,’ Sami hissed, jerking his head at me. ‘She threw a rock at my car window. It’s all smashed. And look at my arm!’

He brandished his arm in his mother’s face, blood trickling down it. His mother gasped as though it was a gunshot wound.

Mina Aunty had caught up by then. ‘Nadia, where have you been? What’s going on?’ she asked.

‘What’s going on is, my son’s going to need stitches because of this girl!’ Sami’s mother pointed a thick finger at me.

‘I was trying to get him to stop!’ I said.

‘Stop what?’ Mina Aunty asked.

I went to open my mouth but then, from the corner of my eye, I saw Nadia shake her head. Her pinky finger brushed the back of my hand.

‘Stop what, Zara?’ Mina Aunty repeated. ‘Why would you do this?’

I saw it then, the moment Sami’s mother knew. Her eyes flitted to Nadia’s mouth for half a second, her smudged lipstick. When she spoke again, her voice was quieter.

‘Why don’t you take Nadia back inside, Mina?’ she said. ‘We don’t need anyone else coming out here.’

Mina Aunty paused and looked at me for a moment, like she might take me with her. But then she took Nadia’s arm, and they headed to the hall.

As they walked away, Nadia looked back at me. By then, the sky had turned the candlelit dark blue that it only does during the summertime. The lamps had come on, and shadows striped her face. She mouthed something to me, but I couldn’t make it out. Then Mina Aunty tugged her hand and she turned away.

I waited for Nadia to look back again, but she didn’t.

entries.title: Secrets by Bob Woodward review – the world’s most famous reporter reveals all
entries.summary: The journalist who helped bring down Nixon on false starts, Watergate, and the art of cultivating a source‘I have always disliked the term ‘investigative reporter’.” So writes Bob Woodward, one of the most celebrated reporters of our time – the man whose Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein undoubtedly changed the US presidency and journalism itself for ever. entries.content:
‘I have always disliked the term ‘investigative reporter’.” So writes Bob Woodward, one of the most celebrated reporters of our time – the man whose Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein undoubtedly changed the US presidency and journalism itself for ever. His longtime boss, the Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee, disliked the term too: “All reporting is investigative,” Bradlee would say.

The term conjures a certain sophistication, perhaps, but part of the beauty of a reporter’s work is how deceptively unsophisticated it can be. Secrets is a far-ranging, revealing memoir of an extraordinary career, but more than that, it is an ode to grinding it out – knocking on doors, asking and asking again, listening, taking notes, making notes on the notes, patiently following every lead to exhaustion. In a media ecosystem saturated with fast and flimsy takes, this feels like a tonic. The real star of his story, Woodward seems to insist, is the shoe leather.

Secrets was written with his assistant, Claire McMullen, who is credited at length in a preface for making possible “a project in self-discovery for me at age 83”, by playing the role of shrink and interrogator. It turns out Woodward’s drive to uncover the truth began at the age of 11, when he discovered his parents were on the brink of divorce and his mother was having an affair. “You have to snoop, I concluded,” he writes. “You must look everywhere things could be hidden because they are being hidden.” He kept up the habit as a teenager, working as janitor at his father’s law firm, where he had unfettered access to an attic-full of files on the residents of Wheaton, Illinois: documents detailing the never-spoken-of arrests, sexual assaults and disputes of his neighbours. So much was hidden under the surface.

Mark Felt – the FBI source who would later be known as “Deep Throat” – arrives not even 50 pages into this 500-plus-page account, in a chance meeting when Woodward was still in the navy. Woodward began instinctively cultivating Felt well before he even knew he wanted to be a reporter. Was it destiny or simply good intuition and a healthy imagination?

The early years of Woodward’s career unfurl in similarly fateful fashion. His first attempt to get hired at the Washington Post – a two-week tryout, granted thanks to a recommendation from a navy admiral – was a spectacular but exhilarating failure: “I had finally found something that I seemed to really like, even love, doing.” Rejected by the Post, he went to work at the Montgomery Sentinel, where he learned the basics of reporting, then renewed his campaign to join the Post, leaving an “obnoxious” number of phone messages for the metropolitan editor, Harry Rosenfeld. Finally, Rosenfeld’s wife asked: “Isn’t this just the kind of reporter you always say you want to hire?”

As the Post’s lowest-rung journalist, Woodward was assigned a night shift at the DC police headquarters. Then, 10 months into the job, the Democratic party headquarters was burgled. It was off to the races; soon, Robert Redford was calling. After Watergate, Woodward switched focus to other kinds of secrets: in-fighting on the supreme court, the shadowy workings of the CIA, and one White House administration after another. With the publication of each new book – nearly two dozen in total – yet another stronghold of power found itself unpleasantly exposed. “That Woodward’s an evil guy,” was how Bill Clinton put it after the publication of The Agenda: Inside the Clinton White House. Over time, Woodward became something of a Washington institution himself. To receive a call from him, Clinton aide George Stephanopoulos would later note, was to be struck with two simultaneous thoughts: “Oh no! and I have arrived!”

A key tenet of Woodward’s was to take seriously the work of everyone he interviewed. Ordinarily tight-lipped political operatives found it hard to turn down the opportunity to unburden themselves to someone who was really listening, who believed their work mattered. And he was persistent. A typical Woodward tip: “The ideal time to make an unannounced, unscheduled visit for an interview with a general is 8:15pm. They have not gone to bed but they have eaten dinner.”

As his career progressed, he became a target, too. He liked to play cat-and‑mouse games, but so did the Washington insiders he pursued: “Often I believed that I was the cat in the scenario,” Woodward writes, “only to find out later that I had been the mouse all along.” Secrets is entertaining, propulsive and juicy. Sources are named, interview transcripts are reproduced and memos are quoted as, scene by scene, we get to understand the seduction of this kind of work – and its revelatory nature. As one of Woodward’s assistants tells him: “You keep the voice of what Washington actually sounds like when it doesn’t have a teleprompter.”

entries.content:
Very strange things happen in Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel Vaim. A man meets a woman he secretly loved in his youth while running an errand in a nearby town. She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation.

Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laureate’s loosely connected trilogy-in-progress set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. Told in Fosse’s hypnotically recursive style, in a nimble translation by Damion Searls, it is ostensibly a tale of captivity that is only a touch less disorienting than its predecessor, thanks in part to the thematic correspondences it establishes. Beckettian in its relish for the absurd and the tediously mundane, this single-sentence novel opens with a man in his 50s who, for reasons he cannot quite explain, drives to Vaim, and decides to lodge at the empty Vaim Hotel, as yet unaware that he might never leave. Here, too, we have a mysterious female figure before whom male agency fails: Brita, owner of the hotel.

The man, throughout referred to as the Guest, seems to be on the run, although from what or whom we are never told. Indeed, we are given very few facts about him: thrown crumbs that we snatch in the course of his ruminations as well as his reticent interactions with the novel’s slender cast of characters. Besides Brita, these include a shopkeeper and a sailor who is something of a carry-over character from the previous instalment. There is mention of “a woman I used to be married to”. We also know that the man possesses some kind of notoriety, having appeared in the newspapers many years back, and as a result is vaguely familiar to the people he encounters. He is also a believer in God, and either a consummate dissembler, or a true amnesiac. With him are two heavy suitcases, which may or may not mean he intended a long stay. Why Vaim? Has he been before? Does he have family there? He has “no way of knowing for sure”.

On the surface, this tale is not very different from other death-haunted Fosse stories: his God-soaked, seven-volume tour de force, Septology, which can be read as one prolonged moment in the life of an ageing painter meeting his end, or Morning and Evening, about a fisher who wakes up one morning, late in his old age, not immediately realising he is no more. Is Vaim a kind of bardo? Is the man dead or near death? In one scene he watches Brita walk towards him as though she intends to pass right through him. And yet this is not your typical ghost story.

The main drama of the novel concerns the Guest’s tetchy relationship with the nosy and peremptory Brita, his ever-loosening grip on the eerie, off-kilter world around him and the gradual disappearance of his personal effects, from his wallet to his car keys, which appears to be Brita’s doing but could equally be the work of something else altogether. Puzzling over the odd turn events have taken, the man realises he is now a prisoner, condemned to the whims of his host, who is perfectly at ease assigning him little tasks. Without his wallet, he has no ID, and without any way to prove his identity, he has no access to his money in the bank. What currency is he left with, then, but his own freedom? “I think what now, what in the world am I going to do now, here in an unfamiliar hotel, in an unfamiliar place, without money, without, in fact, a car I could drive away in”.

Slippery and disconcerting, this novel could either be Fosse’s idea of trolling his readers, or his most serious work yet. I was torn between feeling that the bizarre atmosphere was cranked up farcically high, and that profound things were being said about the human condition that perhaps couldn’t be said in any other way. Once a person is stripped of everything that tells him who he is, that gives his life meaning, continuity and mobility – his memory, his identity, his material possessions – how much of the self remains? It seems to me the novel suggests that to be is, in some sense, to be held hostage; to exist necessarily in a state of radical passivity before events we cannot control, losses we cannot explain or reverse, and the demands that others make on us.
